summary: Wilde's telegram to Charles Kains-Jackson, using him as his solicitor at the height of the Salomé dispute in November 1893.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote:
Can you come and see me here tomorrow at eleven. Wish to consult you professionally on Salomé business.

OSCAR WILDE
sources.context: Telegram, Wilde to Charles Kains-Jackson, 6 November 1893, 7.32 p.m., St James's Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The editors note that on the verso someone has written 'Reply - that C. K.-J. will keep appointment'. The SALOMÉ business is the dispute over whether Douglas's name should appear as translator on the title page; it was settled by dedicating the play to him instead - 'To my friend Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas, the translator of my play' - after Douglas wrote that the difference was 'between a tribute of admiration from an artist and a receipt from a tradesman'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde used him as his solicitor at the height of the Salomé dispute.

manuscript.repository: William Andrews Clark Memorial Library, UCLA
